## Proposal {.smaller}

Measure `R(f)` with a designed periodic multisine rather than one frequency at a time,
injected through the same photon calibrator and analysed with a measured noise model.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**What would change**

- All in-band frequencies are measured simultaneously within one record
- The DFT is leakage-free, since the record contains an integer number of drive periods
- The per-bin uncertainty is measured from the period-to-period scatter rather than regressed
- The drive spectrum is allocated from the Fisher matrix rather than distributed uniformly
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**What would not change**

- The absolute standard. The excitation is injected through the same Pcal, with the same radiation-pressure traceability
- The exposure to model error. An incorrect parametric model of `C` or `A` produces the same systematic as at present
- The deliverable. The same 68 % envelope on `R(f)`, in the same form used for parameter-estimation marginalisation
:::
:::

The case for the method rests on shape fidelity, measurement time, and robustness to
non-stationarity. It does not rest on absolute accuracy, which is set by Pcal in either case.

::: {.notes}
State the second column early and without hedging. The first question from this audience is
whether the absolute reference is being altered; answering it on the opening slide leaves the
remainder of the talk free to address the measurement itself.

All results shown are Phase 1: a closed-loop DARM twin evaluated against the O4 noise floor
(aligo_O4high, LIGO-T2000012, scaled by the 4 km arm length). No hardware injections appear
anywhere in this deck.
:::

## Notation {.smaller}

$$h(t) = R\,\frac{d_{\rm err}}{L},\qquad R(f) = \frac{1+G}{C},\qquad G = A\,D\,C$$

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
- `C(f,t)` — sensing: optical gain `H_C`, coupled-cavity pole `f_cc`, delay `τ_C`, optical spring, and `κ_C(t)`
- `A(f,t)` — three quadruple-suspension stages (UIM / PUM / TST-ESD), each a scale × shape × delay, tracked by `κ_T` and `κ_PU`
- `D(f)` — digital filters, known to negligible uncertainty
- Pcal — 1047 nm radiation-pressure absolute reference
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
The reported quantity is a 68 % envelope on `R(f)` across 20 Hz – 2 kHz in magnitude and
phase, separating systematic error from statistical uncertainty.

`C` and the per-stage `A_i` are linear time-invariant transfer functions estimated from a
known excitation. This is the problem addressed by frequency-domain system identification.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Notation follows Cahillane et al. 2017 (arXiv:1708.03023) and Sun et al. 2020
(arXiv:2005.02531). This slide establishes shared symbols; it should be brief.
:::

## Calibration uncertainty in O1–O3b {.smaller}

| run | magnitude | phase | reported limiting term |
|---|---|---|---|
| O1 / O2 | ±4.6 % / ±3.0 % | ±2.7° / ±2.0° | Gaussian-process regression residual dominates the budget |
| O3a | < 7 % | < 4° | — |
| O3b | 11.29 % | 9.18° | imperfect frequency-dependent modelling of `R(f)` |
| O4 (target) | < 1 % | < 1° | absolute reference target < 0.1 % / 0.1° |

The O3b budget was limited by the frequency-dependent modelling of `R(f)` — that is, by the
measured shape — rather than by the absolute reference. The present uncertainty estimate
combines an MCMC fit to the reference sweeps with Gaussian-process regression on the
residuals and the TDCF and Pcal distributions, producing 10 000 realisations of `R(f)`; the
regression residual term is the dominant contribution.

::: {.notes}
Sources: O1/O2 Cahillane 2017; O3a Sun 2020; O3b Sun et al. 2021 (arXiv:2107.00129). The O4
row is a target quoted from the low-latency methods preprint (arXiv:2508.08423) and not an
achieved result — say so explicitly. No finalised peer-reviewed O4 systematic-error paper
was found in our literature search.

Present this as the published record, not as a criticism. The relevant observation is
narrow: the term that limited O3b is a shape-measurement term, and a leakage-free estimator
addresses shape measurement.
:::

## Cost of the present measurement {.smaller}

| practice | cost |
|---|---|
| Pcal swept sine — one line, dwell, step | approximately 60 points over 20 Hz–1.2 kHz in about one hour, reaching ~1 % and ~1° over 30 Hz–1.2 kHz; repeated roughly weekly during a run |
| Above 1 kHz | Pcal SNR is low, and single frequencies are driven for several hours each |
| Broadband noise with Welch estimation | the record is not periodic, so the DFT leaks; a sharp roll-off is biased low, and the bias does not average down |
| A one-hour sweep | spans real drift: `f_cc`, the optical gain and ESD charge move during the measurement |

Two points bear on what follows. A broadband Pcal injection already exists — colored random
noise measuring the whole transfer function at once — but it is used as an offline
cross-check outside observation, is not optimised, and is not the primary estimator. And the
O3b limitation was in the measured shape rather than the absolute scale.

::: {.notes}
Karki et al. 2016 (arXiv:1608.05055) for the Pcal sweep practice; Tuyenbayev et al. 2017
(arXiv:1608.05134) for the calibration lines.

The first point needs care. This audience already injects broadband noise, and if the
proposal is understood as a restatement of that practice the discussion ends here. The next
slide draws the distinction.
:::

## Relation to the existing broadband injection {.smaller}

| | existing broadband Pcal injection | periodic multisine |
|---|---|---|
| waveform | colored random noise | exactly periodic multisine |
| DFT | windowed, subject to leakage | synchronous, leakage-free |
| noise model | assumed or averaged | measured from period-to-period scatter |
| spectrum shape | unoptimised | allocated from the Fisher matrix |
| role | offline cross-check, outside observation | candidate primary estimator |

The distinguishing properties are periodicity, which removes leakage; Fisher-based
allocation of the drive spectrum; and a measured per-bin noise covariance. Broadband
excitation on its own is long established.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Our literature search found no prior application of optimal-excitation frequency-domain
identification to gravitational-wave detector calibration. The claim of novelty should be
stated at this precision and no broader.
:::

## The estimator {.smaller}

1. Design a periodic multisine whose power is placed according to the Fisher information.
2. Inject it for an integer number of periods and discard the transient period or periods.
3. Estimate the FRF by a synchronous DFT — the drive period equals the analysis window, so
   the estimate is leakage-free — as a ratio of averages `⟨Y⟩/⟨X⟩`, with the per-bin noise
   covariance obtained from the period-to-period scatter.
4. Fit the parametric model by maximum likelihood using that covariance.
5. Bound the result by the Cramér–Rao bound from the accumulated Fisher information, and
   return that bound to step 1.

The iteration terminates when the fractional parameter uncertainty `σ/θ` reaches its target.

::: {.notes}
Step 3 carries most of the weight. Periodicity is what makes the noise model measured rather
than assumed, and a measured per-bin covariance is the quantity the Gaussian-process
regression currently supplies indirectly. Steps 1 and 5 make the measurement a design
problem rather than a post-processing problem.
:::

## Leakage bias in a windowed estimate {.smaller}

![](figs/leakage.svg){.r-stretch}

A `Q = {{< var leak.Q >}}` mode at equal power over {{< var leak.T >}} s; the linewidth
spans {{< var leak.bins >}} bins. Peak bias is {{< var leak.ms_bias >}}% for the multisine
and {{< var leak.w_bias >}}% for the windowed random estimate. Combined at the peak, the
random estimator is {{< var leak.rmse_ratio >}}× worse in RMSE over
{{< var leak.seeds >}} seeds.

::: {.notes}
The windowed estimate is both biased and noisier, and the bias is the consequential part:
additional averaging does not remove it. Applied to a sharp cavity-pole roll-off, a windowed
estimator misreports the shape systematically.

This figure shows a high-Q suspension mode rather than a cavity pole. The mechanism is the
same, but say so if asked; the DARM-specific demonstration is the R(f) slide later in the
deck.
:::

## Fisher information and drive allocation {.smaller}

For a model `H(f, θ)` measured at lines `fₖ` with drive PSD `Pxx(fₖ)` and noise `Pyy(fₖ)`,

$$
\mathcal{I}(\theta) \;=\; 2T \sum_k \frac{P_{xx}(f_k)}{P_{yy}(f_k)}\,
\mathrm{Re}\!\left[\frac{\partial H}{\partial \theta}^{\!H}\frac{\partial H}{\partial \theta}\right]_{f_k}
$$

and the attainable covariance is `𝓘⁻¹`, the Cramér–Rao bound.

- The information scales as the square of the drive amplitude, so the drive level is a design
  variable rather than a constraint.
- The optimal `Pxx` is not flat. Power concentrates where `∂R/∂θ` is largest: near `f_cc`, at
  the stage crossovers, and where the delay contributes.
- The first pass is prior-robust: the design is averaged over the prior range of the
  parameters, so an inaccurate starting model remains covered.

::: {.notes}
The second point is the operative one here. The Pcal force budget is fixed and is presently
distributed by hand; the Fisher matrix determines where an additional increment of drive
produces the largest reduction in σ(R(f)) for the reported parameters.
:::

## Optimal and flat drive allocation compared {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](figs/optimal-design.svg)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](figs/convergence.svg)
:::
:::

Gold denotes the Fisher-optimal multisine; grey denotes an equal-power flat drive, included
as a baseline. The CRB variance-reduction factor at equal power and record length is
F = {{< var head.F >}}, corresponding to {{< var head.sigma_ratio >}}× smaller parameter
uncertainty at fixed drive, or equal uncertainty at {{< var head.rms_drop >}}× lower drive
amplitude.

::: {.notes}
The second form is the one of operational interest for calibration: the same uncertainty at
reduced force on the test mass. F is computed from fisher.parameter_covariance as the ratio
of worst-diagonal CRB variances at identical power and record length; it is not a fitted
quantity.
:::

## Calibration of the quoted uncertainty {.smaller}

![](figs/crb-pull.svg){.r-stretch}

Over {{< var pull.seeds >}} independent realisations, the normalised errors
`(fit − true)/σ_CRB` are consistent with 𝒩(0,1): empirical σ = {{< var pull.std >}}, mean
{{< var pull.mean >}}. The maximum-likelihood fit attains the bound, so the quoted
uncertainty is the realised one.

::: {.notes}
This result underlies every uncertainty quoted subsequently. For this audience it also
indicates how the method would enter the uncertainty budget: the CRB is a calibrated
statistical envelope and can be propagated into the existing R(f) realisation machinery in
place of the regression residual term.
:::

# DARM {.divider}

## The DARM twin {.smaller}

Sensing `C` from a coupled detuned cavity with delay, three-stage actuation
`κ_UIM / κ_PUM / κ_TST`, the derived servo `D`, and the response

$$ R(f) \;=\; \frac{1 + G(f)}{C(f)}, \qquad G = C\,D\,A $$

Pcal serves as the absolute reference: the ratio `H_stage / H_pcal` cancels the sensing
function, so the actuation strengths are recovered independently of sensing drift.

The pipeline is unchanged from the suspension case: periodic multisine, leakage-free
reference FRF with a measured per-bin covariance, maximum-likelihood fit, Cramér–Rao bound.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Parameters are representative of Advanced LIGO; the noise floor is the O4 curve
`aligo_O4high` (LIGO-T2000012) scaled by the 4 km arm length. The injected drive amplitude
is representative rather than measured, so absolute σ levels are illustrative. The scalings
demonstrated — `1/√T` convergence and agreement with the CRB — do not depend on it.
:::

## Band coverage per unit time {.smaller}

![](figs/darm-sweep.svg){.r-stretch}

One {{< var darm.sweep_T >}} s multisine record covers
[{{< var darm.sweep_bins >}} bins]{.num}. In the same wall-clock time a four-period-dwell
sweep reaches {{< var darm.sweep_pts >}} points, and matching the multisine's band coverage
requires approximately {{< var darm.sweep_cover_h >}} h. Both are evaluated on the same

::: {.notes}
State the comparison precisely. The individual sweep points are tight, because each spends
the full drive power at one frequency; the multisine advantage is in coverage per unit time,
not in per-point uncertainty. Overstating this invites a correct objection.
:::

## A drifting actuation strength {.smaller}

![](figs/darm-drift.svg){.r-stretch}

A {{< var darm.drift_amp >}} %/hour drift on the TST stage over {{< var darm.span_min >}}
minutes, sampled by {{< var darm.n_snap >}} leakage-free records. The plant drifts on a
timescale far longer than one record, so each record is locally stationary.

::: {.notes}
The framing is that drift is a parameter to identify rather than a nuisance to be
re-measured away. A one-hour sweep incorporates drift into the measured shape; a sequence of
short leakage-free records separates the two.
:::

## Tracking residual against the bound

![](figs/darm-tracking.svg){.r-stretch}

`κ(t) = Σ cₖ bₖ(t)` in a Legendre time basis — a Lataire–Pintelon basis expansion in
two-step form. The coefficient covariance `(BᵀWB)⁻¹` is the Cramér–Rao bound on `κ(t)` and
`κ̇(t)`.

## Joint recovery of several drifting parameters

![](figs/darm-joint.svg){.r-stretch}

Optical gain, SRC detuning and a stage `κ` drifting together under a correlated random walk,
recovered jointly, each within its own CRB band. The correlation matrix of the joint fit
indicates which drifts are separable.

::: {.notes}
The correlation matrix is worth dwelling on. It gives a computed answer to whether κ_C and
f_cc drift can be distinguished, which is a live question in the TDCF reconstruction.
:::

## Fisher-optimal placement of the TDCF lines {.smaller}

![](figs/darm-callines.svg){.r-stretch}

A-optimal calibration-line placement, chosen where the joint drift estimate is sharpest. The
same Fisher argument applies to continuously running TDCF lines as to a single sweep: line
frequencies and amplitudes follow from the Fisher matrix for the reported parameters, under
the available Pcal budget.

::: {.notes}
This is the lowest-friction route into operations. It does not replace the sweep; it
re-derives where the permanent lines should sit. If the sweep comparison meets resistance,
this is the more modest proposal to fall back on.
:::

## Resolvability of the drift {.smaller}

| quantity | value |
|---|---|
| injected drift amplitude | {{< var darm.drift_amp >}}% of `κ` |
| per-record σ_κ | {{< var darm.snap_sigma >}}% of `κ` |
| tracking σ_κ from the basis fit | {{< var darm.track_sigma >}}% of `κ` |
| ratio of amplitude to tracking σ | [{{< var darm.resolve >}}×]{.num} |
| local-stationarity error (record ÷ drift timescale) | {{< var darm.local_stat >}}% |

The drift is resolved by a computed factor rather than by inspection. We do not describe a
result as limited without first computing the bound that would establish the limit.

![](figs/srm-diag.svg){.r-stretch}

The same pipeline applied to an SRM HSTS through production foton damping banks:

:::

# Limitations {.divider}

## Where the method offers no improvement {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
### Absolute scale

The absolute reference is Pcal in either case, and the method offers no improvement to it.
The O4 Pcal uncertainty of 0.3 % / 0.15 % is unchanged.
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
### Model error

An incorrect parametric model of `C` or `A` produces the same systematic error as the
swept-sine measurement, since the same model is fitted. A leakage-free estimate is not a
model-free one.
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
### In-band comb

The excitation places a comb of lines in the observation band, more than the four or five
presently running. This is the method's principal operational cost, and one the swept sine
largely avoids during observation.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
Possible mitigations, in order of preference: restricting the measurement to non-observing
time, as the existing broadband cross-check already is; exploiting the known drive phase to
subtract the lines; or confining the comb to the periodic full measurement while leaving the
continuous TDCF lines unchanged.

The footprint — line count, amplitudes, duty cycle and subtractability — must be specified
and shown to be acceptable, or the method remains restricted to non-observing time.
:::

::: {.notes}
Do not understate this. The cost is evident to anyone in this audience within a minute, and
conceding it directly is what makes the remainder of the argument credible. If pressed, the
accurate answer is that we do not know the acceptable footprint and that defining it is part
of what we are asking for.
:::

## Comparison on the calibration figures of merit {.smaller}

| figure of merit | swept sine | periodic multisine | assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| `σ(R(f))` shape bias | windowed estimate near `f_cc` | leakage-free | favours the multisine, subject to demonstration |
| time to reach that σ | ~1 hr for ~60 points; hours per point above 1 kHz | all bins within one record | favours the multisine, most strongly above 1 kHz |
| in-band contamination | four to five lines, subtractable | a comb of lines | favours the swept sine |
| non-stationarity | a one-hour sweep spans real drift | one short, locally stationary record | favours the multisine |
| statistical / systematic separation | MCMC with a regression residual term | measured per-bin σ giving a CRB envelope | favours the multisine, conditional on the model |
| exposure to model error | present | identical | no difference |
| Pcal traceability | 0.3–0.15 % (O4) | unchanged, same Pcal | no difference |

## Outstanding validation {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**The efficiency claim is empirical.** Distributing power across a comb reduces the per-bin
SNR; the advantage arises from simultaneity, Fisher-based allocation and leakage-free
estimation. Whether the net `σ(R(f))` per unit time improves on the swept sine must be
measured on the same interferometer state.

**The comb footprint** must be specified and shown to be acceptable, failing which the
method is restricted to non-observing time.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Several citations require verification** before circulation: the author list and venue of
the O4 low-latency preprint; Bhattacharjee 2022; Vitale 2021 and Payne 2020; the first
author of the Cramér–Rao requirements paper; and the O3a calibration-line table and equation
numbers in Tuyenbayev and Sun against the published texts.

**The twin is a twin.** A single DARM loop with a representative drive amplitude and no
interferometer cross-couplings. It demonstrates the measurement, not a calibration of any
instrument.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
This slide is included deliberately. A method described together with its unverified
citations and unproven claims is more defensible than one presented without them.
:::

## Proposed test {.smaller}

A single non-observing window, using the existing photon calibrator, with no additional
hardware.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
1. You select the interferometer state and the window.
2. We design the multisine against your current best `C` and `A` model and the available
   Pcal force limit.
3. The excitation is injected through the same Pcal presently in use.
4. A swept sine is run the same day on the same state.
5. The two `σ(R(f))` envelopes are compared per unit measurement time.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
We would provide the pipeline — excitation design, leakage-free FRF, per-bin noise model,
maximum-likelihood fit and Cramér–Rao bound — as implemented and tested against the O4 noise
floor.

We would need from you the interferometer state, the window, the Pcal drive limit, the
acceptable comb footprint, and an assessment of the result.

If the multisine envelope does not improve on the swept sine, that is a useful result.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the request the talk is built around. It is deliberately small: a single
non-observing window is a far more tractable proposition than a change to the calibration
procedure, and a direct comparison is in any case the only thing that settles the efficiency
question.

The more modest alternative, if the sweep comparison meets resistance, is A-optimal
placement of the permanent TDCF lines, which requires no operational change.
:::

## Summary {.smaller}

- A periodic multisine with a synchronous DFT removes leakage bias and yields a measured
  per-bin noise model, which can be propagated in place of the regression residual term.
- Fisher-based allocation of the drive gives {{< var head.sigma_ratio >}}× smaller parameter
  uncertainty at fixed drive, or equal uncertainty at {{< var head.rms_drop >}}× lower drive.
- The maximum-likelihood fit attains the Cramér–Rao bound (pull σ = {{< var pull.std >}}),
  so the bound is usable as a stopping rule.
- On DARM: `R(f)` recovered with a measured CRB envelope; one {{< var darm.sweep_T >}} s
  record covers {{< var darm.sweep_bins >}} bins, where the sweep requires approximately
  {{< var darm.sweep_cover_h >}} h for the same coverage; a {{< var darm.drift_amp >}} %/hour
  drift in `κ` is tracked with a resolvability ratio of {{< var darm.resolve >}}.
- Unchanged: the Pcal standard, the exposure to model error, and the reported deliverable.
- The principal cost is an in-band comb, whose acceptable footprint remains to be defined.

We are asking for one non-observing window, the existing Pcal, and a same-day swept sine for
comparison.

# Backup {.divider}

## Detecting a pole or zero the model does not have {.smaller}

The measured per-bin covariance is what makes this tractable. Because it comes from the
period-to-period scatter rather than from the fit, the residual has an **absolute scale**: it
can be compared against a noise level that was established independently of the model. In an
ordinary least-squares fit the two are not separable, and an inadequate model simply inflates
the inferred noise.

P&S prescribe three checks on a converged fit (§12.3.6, p. 477):

| test | statistic | what it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| per-entry FRF comparison (12-34) | `\|G(θ̂) − Ĝ\| ≤ √(F_p(2,2dof))·σ̂_Ĝ` at ~p% of bins | *where* — a missing pole fails at a contiguous run of bins, not scattered ones |
| cost vs expectation | SML cost is ~χ² with known dof | *whether* — a minimum that is too large indicates undermodeling |
| whiteness of the residuals | autocorrelation of `Ĝ − G(θ̂)` along frequency | *whether it is structured* — noise is uncorrelated between bins; a missing resonance is not |

Order selection and the over- versus under-modelling trade-off are Ch 11 §11.3–§11.4;
overmodelling is controlled by a complexity penalty on the cost.

::: {.notes}
The first sentence is the one that matters, and it is worth saying slowly. The reason this
works is the measured noise model — the same property that lets the CRB be a real envelope
rather than a relative one.

Cited from the repo's P&S index; the book is not reproduced anywhere in this project.
:::

## The whiteness test, on a fit that is missing a mode {.smaller}

![](figs/whiteness.svg){.r-stretch}

A two-mode plant fitted with **one** mode, against the correctly ordered fit on the same data
and the same measured noise. Correct order: lag-1 autocorrelation
{{< var wh.acf1_good >}} against a 95 % band of {{< var wh.bound >}}, portmanteau
p = {{< var wh.p_good >}}, residual power {{< var wh.powratio_good >}}× expected. Undermodelled:
lag-1 autocorrelation [{{< var wh.acf1_bad >}}]{.num}, and the worst residual window falls at
**{{< var wh.worst_lo >}}–{{< var wh.worst_hi >}} Hz**, bracketing the {{< var wh.missing >}} Hz
mode the model omits.

::: {.notes}
Two implementation points, if asked.

The reference for the residual power is not 1 but dof/(dof−n_y): whitening by a SAMPLE
covariance over a finite number of periods inflates it, by the same factor P&S apply to the
expected cost. Comparing against 1 would flag every good fit.

No parameter correction is applied to the chi-squared dof. The Box–Pierce correction subtracts
the order of an ARMA model fitted to the tested series, not the plant's parameter count;
subtracting the latter rejects correct fits.

The test is `system_ident.mimo_fit.whiteness_test`, covered by unit tests that assert both
directions — a correct fit passes, an undermodelled one is caught and localised.
:::

## Applying it to DARM, and where it is weak {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Localising a candidate to sensing or actuation costs nothing extra.** The stage ratio
`H_stage/H_pcal` cancels `C`. So an unmodelled *sensing* feature — an optical spring, a
detuning term — appears in the Pcal FRF and cancels in the stage ratio; an unmodelled
*actuation* feature does the opposite. Which one shows the anomaly identifies the side of the
loop before anything is fitted.

**The unexcited lines are free.** Every bin the multisine does not drive reads the floor
directly, and anything appearing there is not the plant responding.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**The caveat, stated plainly (11-5, p. 434).** The residual-variance compensation
`var(G_meas − G_model) = σ²_G(k) − σ²_G(θ̂)` can go **negative** at sharp resonances, where the
model is flexible and rides only one or two data points. Residual significance cannot be judged
there.

So the residual test is weakest exactly where a sharp unmodelled feature would hide — at a
cavity pole or an optical spring. It is a real limitation of the check, not of the estimator,
and the mitigation is line placement: put lines across the suspect linewidth and re-test.
:::
:::

Once a candidate is localised, the Fisher machinery decides where to place lines to confirm and
pin it. Detection feeding the next excitation design is the part a swept sine cannot do.

::: {.notes}
If someone asks the obvious follow-up — "so you would have missed it too" — the honest answer
is that the test is weakest at sharp features, that this is why the check is not the only one,
and that the design loop exists precisely to spend the next measurement where the evidence is
ambiguous.

Distinguishing an unmodelled LINEAR feature from a nonlinearity is a separate question with its
own machinery: excite only odd harmonics and look for energy at non-excited lines (Ch 3, Ch 4).
Not implemented here.
:::
